key_facts: **AGEP** is a pustular drug reaction: hundreds of tiny **non-follicular** sterile pustules on red, swollen skin, with fever.
Starts in the flexures and face **within hours to 2 days** of an antibiotic (aminopenicillins, macrolides) or other drug (hydroxychloroquine, diltiazem, terbinafine).
Neutrophilia is common; organ involvement is mild and uncommon.
Stop the drug, potent topical steroid and supportive care; settles in **1–2 weeks** with peeling.
Main differential: generalised pustular psoriasis (history of psoriasis, slower course).

sections.title: Overview
blocks: **AGEP** (acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis) is an abrupt eruption of **sterile, non-follicular pinhead pustules** on oedematous erythema. It is usually self-limiting; mortality is under 5%.

sub: Rare (about 1–5 per million per year); any age; more women.

ul: Type IVd reaction: drug-specific T cells release **IL-8 (CXCL8)**, recruiting neutrophils into the epidermis.
Latency **under 48 hours** for antibiotics; up to 1–2 weeks for some drugs.
IL36RN variants overlap with generalised pustular psoriasis.
**"Pustules mean infection"**: AGEP pustules are sterile; more antibiotics can make it worse.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Drug-specific T cells summon **neutrophils** into the top of the epidermis.

mech.t: Drug-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T cells migrate into the epidermis.
T cells and keratinocytes release **IL-8 (CXCL8)** and IL-17.
Neutrophils gather just under the stratum corneum, forming pinhead pustules.
mech.caption: AGEP: neutrophil-filled pustules collect just under the stratum corneum (subcorneal), not around hair follicles, over swollen inflamed skin.

mech.t: As pustules dry, the surface peels in collarettes over 1–2 weeks.

histo: Subcorneal or intraepidermal spongiform pustules, papillary oedema, eosinophils, sometimes necrotic keratinocytes.

ul: Pinhead pustules on erythema, starting in the **flexures and face** and becoming generalised; burning or itch.
Fever above 38 °C; neutrophilia; mild organ involvement in up to 20%.

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: Clinical with history; FBC (neutrophilia), U&E, LFT. Biopsy shows subcorneal or intraepidermal spongiform pustules (to distinguish it from pustular psoriasis). The EuroSCAR score helps. Patch testing later.

sections.title: Differential diagnoses
blocks: **Generalised pustular psoriasis** (history of psoriasis, slower onset, longer course), subcorneal pustular dermatosis, pustular DRESS, folliculitis, SJS/TEN (early AGEP can show Nikolsky-like sloughing).

ul: **Stop the drug**, document, Yellow Card, avoid for life.
Potent topical steroid; antipyretics; supportive care. Systemic steroids are rarely needed.
Usually managed in dermatology, with admission if unwell.

ladder.t: Stop the culprit; record allergy; Yellow Card.

refer.t: Widespread pustules with fever within days of a new drug.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Widespread pustules within days of an antibiotic: **same-day dermatology**.
Mucosal erosions, skin sloughing or systemic organ dysfunction: hospital.
Superinfection; rarely liver, kidney or lung involvement; fluid loss in frail patients.
Excellent once the drug is stopped; recurs on re-exposure.

pearls: AGEP has the **shortest latency** of the severe drug reactions (hours to 2 days).

quiz.q: What is the typical latency of AGEP after an antibiotic?
Which cytokine drives the neutrophils in AGEP?

quiz.a: Over 1–2 weeks with collarette desquamation after stopping the drug.
